first_impression.reaction: My mum asked if I'm doing 'something old, something new', so I Googled it. I was expecting a twee listicle. The second paragraph changed my mind: 'Then it turns to the choices that matter when the wedding is overseas: which heirloom to wear, what to commission, who to borrow from, and how to carry irreplaceable pieces safely across the world.' That last bit is a real question for us, so I kept going. No 'fairytale' anywhere, thank god.

journey.quote: Carry heirlooms, borrowed pieces and the sixpence in your hand luggage, photograph them before you fly, and check your travel insurance's per-item limits.
journey.reaction: That's the one line I'd screenshot for Mum. Practical, and it's what I'd actually forget.

journey.quote: Partners of any gender can carry any of the five, and plenty of couples share them between the two outfits.
journey.reaction: Good. James can carry something too, and it doesn't make a big deal of saying so.

journey.section: 2. Where the rhyme was first printed
journey.quote: The book is about Shropshire, but the rhyme is given there as the saying of friends from Lancashire.
journey.reaction: Nice trivia for a speech, but I skimmed most of this section. It reads confidently and I'd quote it to my parents. Not why I'd hire anyone though.

journey.quote: Have a jeweller check clasps and settings a few months before the wedding, so nothing gives way on the day.
journey.reaction: Exactly the kind of small, specific tip that makes me think someone has seen a brooch fall off at a ceremony.

journey.quote: Agree with the family before anything is reset. A grandmother may love the idea, or may want the ring to stay as she wore it.
journey.reaction: Honest and a bit wise. This is precisely the family politics I'd want to get ahead of.

journey.quote: Allow time. A commissioned piece needs design meetings, a making period and a final fitting, so start several months before you travel.
journey.reaction: We're 14 months out, so this is useful timing. I like that it says 'before you travel', not 'before the wedding'.

journey.quote: Agree with the owner how the piece will travel, who carries it and when it goes back, and return it in person after the wedding.
journey.reaction: This is the stuff that goes wrong with 80 people overseas. Good. But who actually keeps track of it on the day, us?

journey.quote: For a destination wedding, choose blue that survives a long-haul flight.
journey.reaction: Ha, very true. Stitched initials in James's jacket lining is going on the list.

journey.quote: Either way, a coin under the heel for hours is uncomfortable, so many couples tape it inside the shoe, tuck it under the insole or carry it in a pocket instead.

journey.section: 8. Modern and luxury ways to do all four
journey.quote: One piece from each side. Something old from one family, something borrowed from the other, so both are in the room.
journey.reaction: Love this. Both sets of parents are contributing, and this is a tasteful way to include both without it feeling try-hard.

journey.section: 8. Modern and luxury ways to do all four
journey.quote: These are the combinations we see work best:
journey.reaction: 'We see' implies you've done lots of these. I'd believe it more with one real wedding, venue and date, where a family piece travelled overseas.

journey.section: 9. Carrying heirlooms to a destination wedding
journey.quote: Standard travel insurance policies typically don't cover items stolen from checked baggage on an airline, train or bus.
journey.reaction: Didn't know that. As a lawyer I like that it points me to the PDS rather than hand-waving.

journey.section: 9. Carrying heirlooms to a destination wedding
journey.quote: A borrowed piece belongs to someone else, so ask the owner whether their own contents policy covers it overseas before it leaves home.
journey.reaction: Insider-level thinking. My aunt's veil would be exactly this situation.

journey.quote: A Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments around the day, as your single point of contact.
journey.reaction: Single point of contact answers 'who's accountable'. But does that person also help with the heirloom side, like the hotel safe and getting pieces to the getting-ready room? It doesn't say.

journey.quote: Something borrowed is lucky when it has been worn by a happily married bride.
journey.reaction: I've now read this point about four times on one page. Skimmed the FAQ.

journey.quote: The fee is agreed in writing before any work begins, and your advisor confirms the inclusions in writing before you commit.
journey.reaction: Good, that speaks to hidden costs. Nothing here about currency or quoting in AUD though.

unanswered_questions: Is there a real wedding with a venue and date where a family heirloom or borrowed veil travelled overseas?
Does the Wedded Advisor help with the heirloom logistics on the day (hotel safe, who holds what, getting pieces to the getting-ready room and back)?
Is the fee quoted in AUD, and how are currency changes handled for overseas vendors?
Can the advisor connect us with a jeweller or tailor for a commission or a reset, or is that on us?
would_share_with: James (partner): the something blue ideas and the cufflinks
My mum (the one who asked): the full rhyme, borrowed veil and the 'one piece from each side' idea
James's parents: carrying heirlooms and the insurance section

cta_reaction.why: Low pressure and the written fee is reassuring, but I came here for a tradition, not a planner. I'd bookmark the magazine and read a destination post and a real wedding before enquiring.

top_3_changes: Link a real wedding from your pages, with venue and date, where a family piece travelled overseas, to back up 'the combinations we see work best'.
Say in one line what the Wedded Advisor does for heirlooms and borrowed pieces on the day (safe storage, who holds what, returns).
Trim the FAQ repetition of the 'happily married bride' point so the end of the page reads tighter.
